headline: Thinking Machines releases first open AI model, Inkling
summary: Mira Murati's startup launches Inkling, a 975B parameter open-weight model designed for customization, challenging one-size-fits-all AI.
details: Thinking Machines, founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, has unveiled its first proprietary AI model, Inkling. Unlike closed models from major labs, Inkling is open-weight, allowing external developers to download and modify it directly.

Inkling is a mixture-of-experts system with 975 billion total parameters, utilizing about 41 billion for any given task to maintain speed and efficiency. It was trained on 45 trillion tokens of text, image, audio, and video, with native reasoning capabilities across all modalities.

The model is designed to provide calibrated answers, flag uncertainty, and allows users to adjust 'thinking effort' for a trade-off between speed and depth. On one benchmark, Inkling reportedly used a third of the tokens of Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra for equivalent coding performance.

Thinking Machines positions Inkling not as a best-in-class model, but as a well-rounded starting point for organizations to fine-tune via its Tinker platform. This approach contrasts with general-purpose chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.

The company argues that AI organizations can adapt themselves outperforms centralized, one-size-fits-all models. This philosophy is gaining traction, with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warning enterprises about the hidden costs of proprietary AI models.

Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue also predicts a shift towards private or open-source alternatives for most production AI work, with frontier models reserved for specialized tasks. This aligns with Thinking Machines' strategy.

Evidence for this trend comes from a project with Bridgewater Associates, where an open-source model fine-tuned on their financial expertise outperformed proprietary models on financial reasoning tests at a fraction of the cost.

headline_marked: Apple [[reportedly shopping for AI chip companies]] to bolster server power
headline: Apple reportedly shopping for AI chip companies to bolster server power
summary: Sources say Apple is in talks with semiconductor makers and bankers to acquire companies, facing performance issues with its M2 Ultra chips for AI tasks.
details: Apple is reportedly exploring acquisitions of AI chip companies as it seeks to enhance its server infrastructure. The company has allegedly faced performance limitations with its M2 Ultra chips for certain AI computations, leading it to consider bolstering its capabilities through strategic purchases.

While Apple typically doesn't make large acquisitions, its AI ambitions might necessitate a shift in strategy. The company is said to be in discussions with semiconductor manufacturers and investment bankers regarding potential targets to strengthen its AI processing power.

Performance issues have been noted with servers running on Apple's M2 Ultra chips for AI tasks. For more intensive AI workloads, such as those powering Gemini models for Siri, Apple reportedly relies on NVIDIA chips hosted on Google Cloud.

The development of Apple's own next-generation server chip, codenamed "Baltra," has reportedly faced delays, with an M7 Ultra-based server chip not expected until 2029. However, an upgrade to M5 Ultra chips is anticipated soon.

Apple's expertise in chip design has historically focused on consumer devices. The company's past acquisition of PA Semi in 2008 for $278 million marked its entry into custom chip manufacturing. More recently, it acquired AI startup Q.ai for nearly $2 billion.

The acquisition of AI chip companies could come at a premium, given the critical role of specialized hardware in the AI sector. However, Apple possesses substantial financial resources, with $45.6 billion in cash and cash equivalents as of late March, providing flexibility for such strategic moves.
